newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn denies interfering in British affairs.
newsitem.headline: Bonn denies interfering in British affairs.

text.p: Germany on Monday denied interfering in British affairs by calling on Britain to clarify its European stance in a forthcoming general election, and said a statement by Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel was an expression of goodwill.
But a ministry spokesman also said the idea of interference in another country's affairs was anyway less and less relevant in a growing political union.

"In a European Union which aspires to become a political union, interference in (another's) internal affairs is by definition hardly possible," spokesman Martin Erdmann told a government news conference. "But even if it were possible, it is certainly not intended...
"In connection with important EU decisions to be taken in 1997, the election in Britain is an important component, but it is first and foremost the concern of the British themselves."
"(Kinkel's comment) is a political declaration of goodwill towards Britain," he added.
Kinkel, in a New Year statement, drew attention to the British election at the top of a list of events likely to shape German foreign policy in 1997.
He said Britain must now reach a clear decision on its European Union policy -- prompting a number of British politicians to call the remarks unhelpful and say Britons would make up their own minds.

The issue of closer European integration is especially sensitive for the ruling Conservatives, who have several times seen open revolt within their own ranks from "euro-sceptics" opposed to greater European integration.

But Erdmann dismissed the suggestion that Kinkel's comment had any party political character while urging Britain, traditionally wary of relinquishing any part of its sovereignty, to take on Germany's vision of deeper integration in the EU.

"Britain must become clear on what depth of integration it wants to reach, and as (Kinkel) said, we want Britain to be among those countries which, together with others, achieve as deep an integration as possible," Erdmann said.

Kinkel's statement included an affirmation that the planned single currency -- one of the most controversial aspects of EU membership for Britain -- would go ahead and that preparations would continue through 1997.

He also called for renewed efforts to ensure the success of efforts currently in progress to streamline EU decision-making and reduce individual countries' veto powers -- another source of irritation to British euro-sceptics.
